# Factorize

Hosted workflow: connect your agent → define Events → attach Triggers → subscribe to durable occurrences.

Application: https://app.factorize.sh
MCP (Streamable HTTP + OAuth): https://app.factorize.sh/mcp

Browser: manage Event definitions, input Triggers, integrations and consent.
MCP: discover Events, subscribe to occurrence resources, read durable occurrences, and manage Triggers.
A resource update notification signals that an occurrence is ready to read; stored occurrences support recovery after reconnecting.

Generated from maintained guides in navigation order. Do not edit this file directly.

## Factorize with your agent
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/

Factorize stores versioned Event definitions, input Triggers, and durable Event
occurrences. MCP subscribers receive notifications when an occurrence is
available and can read it later.

Start at [app.factorize.sh](https://app.factorize.sh), connect an MCP client to
`https://app.factorize.sh/mcp`, create an Event and attach one or more Triggers.


  [Connect your agent](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/overview): Authorize a remote MCP client
  [First Event](https://docs.factorize.sh/quickstart): Create an Event, fire a Trigger, and read the occurrence


See [concepts](https://docs.factorize.sh/concepts) for the Event model and [self-hosting](https://docs.factorize.sh/self-hosting/deployment)
for deployment information.

## Connect your agent
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/overview

Use Factorize's remote Streamable HTTP endpoint:

```text
https://app.factorize.sh/mcp
```

Configure the endpoint in your MCP client and complete its OAuth flow. Authorize
`triggers:read` to discover Events and read occurrences. Authorize
`triggers:write` to create Events and Triggers, configure sources, and fire a
manual Trigger. Other scopes apply only to their corresponding integrations or
application operations.

Ask your client to call `list_events` and `list_triggers`. An empty list is a
successful connection to a workspace without configured Events or Triggers.

## Event subscriptions

MCP clients can subscribe to an Event occurrence resource. When a Trigger
publishes a validated occurrence, the server sends a resource-updated
notification. Read the resource to obtain the durable occurrence data. A client
that reconnects can use `list_event_occurrences` or the corresponding REST
endpoint to recover stored occurrences.

## Built-in workflow skills

Factorize publishes built-in MCP Skills with workflow guidance. Use
`skills/list` to discover the catalog and `skills/get` to get the
`manage-triggers` manifest. Read its resource for instructions on managing
Events and Triggers.

## Your first Event
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/quickstart

## Connect an MCP client

Connect to `https://app.factorize.sh/mcp` using the [MCP setup guide](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/overview).
Authorize `triggers:read` to discover Events and occurrences, and `triggers:write`
to create or change Events and Triggers.

## Create and publish an Event

An Event defines the payload shape. A Trigger belongs to one Event and watches
an input source. Multiple Triggers may publish to the same Event.

Use the `create_event` MCP tool or the REST API to create an Event named `review.requested`
with a JSON object payload schema. Then call `create_trigger` to add an enabled Trigger attached to it.
For a simple local check, create a manual Trigger and fire it with a stable
idempotency key and a JSON payload accepted by the Event schema.

```json
{
  "eventId": "EVENT_ID",
  "name": "manual-review",
  "sources": [{ "kind": "manual", "config": {} }]
}
```

## Subscribe, fire, and read

Call `list_events` or `get_event` to find the Event ID. Subscribe to
`factorize://events/{eventId}/occurrences` before firing the Trigger.

Call `fire_trigger` with `triggerId`, `idempotencyKey`, and `data`. The response
includes the durable occurrence ID. Reusing the same idempotency key returns
that ID and reports a duplicate.

Read the resource after the MCP update notification. After reconnecting, use
`list_event_occurrences` to recover occurrences that arrived while disconnected.

The same data is available from `GET /api/v1/events/{eventId}/occurrences`.

## Create and edit Triggers
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/work/triggers

A Trigger belongs to exactly one Event. An Event can have multiple Triggers.
Triggers accept supported input sources such as schedules, signed webhooks,
provider events, and explicit fire requests. A match produces a durable
occurrence of the parent Event; it does not start an agent execution.

Use the browser or MCP `create_trigger` and `update_trigger` tools. Each Trigger
has a name, an `eventId`, and a `sources` array with a kind and configuration for
each source. Updates replace the configuration, so read the current Trigger
first and include the intended full configuration. Credentials are configured through integrations and are never
accepted in Trigger input.

## Sources and delivery

- **Schedule:** cron expression and timezone.
- **Webhook/provider:** provider-specific routing configuration, signatures,
  conditions and delivery identifiers.
- **Manual:** `fire_trigger` with a payload and idempotency key.

Duplicate provider deliveries and repeated manual keys do not create duplicate
occurrences. The Event's current JSON payload schema is validated before an
occurrence is stored. Occurrences retain the schema revision used at creation.

See [the Event walkthrough](https://docs.factorize.sh/quickstart), [MCP tools](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/tools), and
[webhook troubleshooting](https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/events).

## Event payloads and conditions
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/events

An Event has a versioned JSON payload schema. Every Trigger attached to that
Event publishes an occurrence only when its resulting payload passes the current
schema. Stored occurrences keep their schema revision and payload.

Webhook Triggers can include conditions evaluated against prepared provider
context. The condition preview tool evaluates example data only; it does not
authenticate, route, or publish an occurrence. Repeated delivery IDs are
idempotent. Inspect safe outcomes with `list_trigger_webhook_activity` and
`list_webhook_deliveries`.

MCP subscribers receive resource update notifications after an occurrence is
stored. Notifications indicate that the resource changed; clients read the
resource or list occurrences to obtain durable data.

## GitHub Triggers
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/github

Connect a GitHub installation, then attach a GitHub source Trigger to an Event.
Choose the installation, repository, webhook event, action, and optional
conditions in the Trigger configuration. Factorize verifies webhook signatures
and deduplicates provider delivery IDs before validating and storing the Event
occurrence.

Inspect safe delivery outcomes with `list_trigger_webhook_activity` and
`list_webhook_deliveries`. Use [Event payload and condition guidance](https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/events)
for payload validation and [troubleshooting](https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/events) for
rejected or missing deliveries.

## ClickUp Triggers
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/clickup

Connect ClickUp and attach a ClickUp source Trigger to an Event. Select the
workspace resources and match rules in the browser editor. Matching signed
webhook deliveries produce validated durable occurrences; duplicate delivery
IDs are ignored.

Inspect safe delivery outcomes with `list_trigger_webhook_activity` and
`list_webhook_deliveries`. See [Event payloads and conditions](https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/events)
and [troubleshooting](https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/events).

## Integration access
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/oauth

Integrations hold server-side credentials used to validate provider webhooks or
make authorized API requests. Select only the integrations needed for your
Triggers or MCP connection. Credentials are encrypted and never returned by
Factorize APIs.

Bearer API, GitHub, Linear, ClickUp, X, Fly.io, exe.dev, Amp, and Cloudflare Tail
integrations have distinct setup flows. Cloudflare Tail is an inbound webhook
signing integration. Use the browser's Integrations page to connect or revoke
credentials and to choose which MCP clients may access them.

Events and Trigger source definitions store references and configuration, not
credentials. Disconnecting an integration can prevent its future input
processing; it does not rewrite already stored Event occurrences.

## Connection problems
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/connection

| Symptom | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Browser consent fails or is cancelled | Sign in to the intended Factorize account, restart authorization from the client, and approve the requested scopes. |
| The authorization link expired or was used | Start **Reconnect** in the MCP client and open its new authorization link. Keep approval in the same browser and Factorize account. If only the consent form expired, reload it and review the choices again. |
| Saved permissions are missing from consent | Open **Clients → Edit permissions** to save your choices, then reconnect the same registered client. If it explicitly requests a scope list, add the missing scopes to that client request. If it omits scope, choose from the Factorize API scopes in the browser. Existing access and refresh tokens cannot gain permissions. |
| Client never connects | Confirm `https://app.factorize.sh/mcp`, remote Streamable HTTP and OAuth support. Open the client's MCP status view and authenticate; see [client-specific instructions](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/overview). |
| `invalid_token` or access disappears | Reauthorize the client. Password reset, password change, or sign-out can invalidate delegated credentials. |
| `insufficient_scope` | Reconnect and grant `triggers:read` to discover Events and occurrences, or `triggers:write` to manage Events and Triggers. Add integration scopes only when needed. |
| Provider input is not arriving | Check the saved integration and Trigger source configuration. For delivery diagnosis, see [Event troubleshooting](https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/events). |

Revoking an MCP authorization affects access but does not delete stored Events,
Triggers, or occurrences. Provider reconnection is separate and can be managed
from the Integrations page.

## Event and Trigger troubleshooting
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/events

## No occurrence was created

1. Confirm that the Trigger is enabled and belongs to the intended Event.
2. Inspect its source configuration and integration connection in the browser.
3. For a webhook, inspect `list_trigger_webhook_activity` and
   `list_webhook_deliveries` for signature, condition, routing, or duplicate
   outcomes. These records omit secrets and raw payloads.
4. Check that the Event's current payload schema accepts the resulting JSON.
5. For manual firing, confirm the Trigger kind and reuse the original
   idempotency key when retrying an uncertain request.

## A subscriber missed a notification

Notifications tell the client that an Event resource changed; they are not the
stored payload. Read the Event resource or call `list_event_occurrences` to
recover durable occurrences after reconnecting. Confirm the client has
`triggers:read` and supports MCP resource subscriptions.

## MCP tool reference
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/tools

Connect to `https://app.factorize.sh/mcp` using [client authorization](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/overview).
Tools return structured JSON. IDs must come from the authorized workspace.

## Events and occurrences

`list_events` and `get_event` discover Event definitions and their payload
schemas. `create_event` and `update_event` manage those definitions. Each Event
may have multiple Triggers. An enabled Trigger publishes an occurrence only
after validating the payload against the Event's current JSON schema.

Subscribe to `factorize://events/{eventId}/occurrences` using MCP resource
subscription support. After a resource-updated notification, read the resource
to retrieve durable data. `list_event_occurrences` lets a reconnecting client
recover stored records.

MCP Events clients discover the stable `factorize.occurrence` type with
`events/list` and subscribe using `arguments: { "event_id": "<uuid>" }`.
Get the UUID from `create_event` or `list_events`; no plugin refresh is
needed for new Event definitions after the one-time catalog refresh. Reuse the
same name, arguments, and callback to renew or unsubscribe. Existing per-Event
subscriptions keep their original names and continue receiving webhooks.
Each notification includes the occurrence and definition IDs. Call
`read_event_occurrences` with `occurrenceId` for the committed payload. For a
wake without an ID, call it with the saved `definitionId` and a recent `since`
time, and follow `nextCursor` with the same definition and time. Windowed reads
use recorded time so recent arrivals with older source timestamps appear.
Reads leave history intact.

`delete_event` permanently removes the Event, all attached Triggers and input
configurations, and all stored occurrences.

## Triggers

A Trigger belongs to one Event and watches a schedule, signed webhook/provider
input, or manual fire request. Duplicate deliveries are deduplicated. Reuse the
same `idempotencyKey` after an uncertain manual fire. Webhook activity tools
show safe processing outcomes without exposing secrets or raw payloads.

`create_trigger` and `update_trigger` require a parent `eventId` and an
explicit `sources` array of input configurations. For a manual-only Trigger,
send `sources: [{ "kind": "manual" }]`. Read a Trigger before replacing its
configuration.

## Integration APIs

Integration tools use server-held credentials and current authorization; credentials are never
returned. `get_api_reflection` describes available integrations and safe request
examples before `request_api` is used. See [REST reference](https://docs.factorize.sh/api/reference) for
exact request and response schemas.

## VM permissions

Use `grant_vm_permissions` to enroll an existing Machine through a team VM
provider connection. Supply the team's integration ID as `providerId`, the
Machine ID as `vm`, and the Fly app name as `app`. Create a request key once and
reuse it for retries. Initial enrollment requires a running Machine with
`curl`, `openssl`, and permission to use the Fly OIDC socket in the guest.

```json
{
  "target": {
    "kind": "machine",
    "providerId": "9dd924e0-3a35-48d5-bcd1-56e4b0922265",
    "vm": "1234abcd",
    "app": "my-app",
    "requestKey": "my-app-workload-1"
  },
  "permissions": { "scopes": ["triggers:read"] }
}
```

Use `permissions.presetId` to apply a preset. Factorize saves its current
scopes and rejects the entire request if any requested scope is outside the
caller's effective access. To replace permissions, supply a `target` with
`kind: "existing"`, `grantId`, and `expectedRevision` from `list_vms`. Revoking
a grant removes its Factorize permissions while the workload keeps running.
Enrollment is available only for providers enabled after identity validation.

### Authenticate from an enrolled Machine

On Fly.io, request an OIDC token through the `/.fly/api` Unix socket. POST
`{"aud":"<grant authentication.audience>"}` to `http://localhost/v1/tokens/oidc`.
Keep the private key in the guest at the returned `authentication.guestKeyPath`,
relative to the enrollment user's home directory.

For each REST or MCP HTTP request, set these headers:

- `Authorization: Bearer <provider OIDC token>`
- `X-Factorize-VM-Grant: <grant ID>`
- `X-Factorize-VM-Proof: <signed proof JWT>`

Sign the proof with the enrolled P-256 private key. Use JWT header fields
`alg: "ES256"` and `typ: "factorize-vm-proof+jwt"`, and encode the signature in
the 64-byte JWS format. Include these claims:

| Claim | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `grant` | Grant ID |
| `ath` | Unpadded base64url SHA-256 of the provider token |
| `htm` | HTTP method |
| `htu` | Absolute request URL, including its query string |
| `jti` | A new UUID for each HTTP request |
| `iat` | Current Unix time in seconds |

Send the proof within 60 seconds and sign a fresh proof for every retry. MCP
workloads need a transport that can set dynamic HTTP headers. The VM uses
the scopes in its saved grant and refreshes its provider token before expiry.

## Events and Triggers
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/concepts

A **team** owns Events, Triggers, integrations, and authorization settings.

An **Event** is a named durable record with a versioned JSON payload schema. A
matching Trigger creates an occurrence, which subscribers can read later. An
Event may have multiple Triggers.

A **Trigger** watches one input source: a schedule, signed webhook, provider
notification, or explicit fire request. Matching and duplicate-delivery checks
happen before Factorize validates and stores the Event occurrence. A Trigger
publishes data; it does not launch an agent or create an execution.

MCP clients discover Event definitions, subscribe to their occurrence resource,
and receive a resource-updated notification after a new occurrence. They then
read the resource to obtain durable data. Occurrences are also available through
the authorized REST API, so a reconnecting client can recover stored data.

## REST API reference
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/api/reference

The **REST operations** group under Reference renders every application operation directly from [openapi.yaml](https://docs.factorize.sh/openapi.yaml), including request validation, required scopes, owner-session restrictions, and JSON response schemas. This is the same generated artifact verified by CI and available to API clients.

All application endpoints use `/api/v1`. Authenticate with a scoped bearer token or an interactive owner session; credential management and trace replay require an interactive owner session. Errors use `{ "error": { "code": "...", "message": "..." } }`.

`GET /healthz` is the unauthenticated infrastructure liveness probe and returns `{ "ok": true }`. It is outside the application API contract.

See [authentication](https://docs.factorize.sh/api/authentication) for access setup and [OpenAPI definition](https://docs.factorize.sh/api/openapi) for downloading or regenerating the contract.

## Authentication and scopes
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/api/authentication

Protected REST and MCP requests use `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Browser
users may also use their signed Factorize session cookie. Access is tenant-bound;
ownership and session version are rechecked on service calls.

## Scopes

| Scope | Allows |
| --- | --- |
| `team:read` | Read team settings |
| `team:write` | Update team settings |
| `triggers:read` | Discover Events, Triggers, and stored occurrences |
| `triggers:write` | Manage Events and Triggers |
| `integrations:read` | Read integration metadata and provider resources |
| `integrations:write` | Manage integration connections |
| `proxy:use` | Use authorized external integration APIs |
| `apps:manage` | Manage registered applications |

Scopes are independent; write does not imply read. Integration-specific scopes
are granted separately. Owner-only operations require an interactive browser
session.

Owners can edit the effective scopes of an existing MCP connection in Settings;
saved scope additions and removals apply immediately. Team permission presets
can preselect scopes during new client authorization.

## OAuth clients

Authorization-code clients must use PKCE S256. Implicit and plain PKCE are
disabled. Access tokens last one hour; refresh tokens can last up to 30 days.
RFC 7009 revocation is advertised by discovery. Device authorization is also
supported for public clients; follow the advertised OAuth metadata and device
verification instructions.

Never send provider credentials to an API client. Stored integration secrets
are used server-side and omitted from responses.

## OAuth discovery
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/api/discovery

At `https://app.factorize.sh`, clients can retrieve:

* `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` — issuer, authorization, token, registration, revocation, and device endpoints plus supported grants/scopes.
* `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` — resource `https://app.factorize.sh/mcp`, authorization server, header bearer authentication, and supported scopes.

The authorization endpoint is `/authorize`, token endpoint `/oauth/token`, dynamic registration endpoint `/oauth/register`, and device endpoint `/oauth/device_authorization`. Client ID Metadata Documents are enabled. MCP clients should use `https://app.factorize.sh/mcp`; they can discover OAuth automatically and complete browser PKCE consent.

## OpenAPI definition
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/api/openapi

[Download openapi.yaml](https://docs.factorize.sh/openapi.yaml). Clients can use this exact file to generate SDKs or inspect request and response schemas.

The definition is generated from the executable route catalog in `packages/api/src/api-contract.ts`, which the Worker dispatches in `protected-api.ts`. To change an API operation, update its catalog entry (method, path, scope, validation, handler, and documentation), then run:

```bash
npm run generate:openapi
```

Commit `packages/docs/openapi.yaml` with the change. CI regenerates it and rejects a diff; parsed contract tests also require exact method/path equality with the executable catalog. Shared schemas and general API metadata live beside the catalog in `trigger-schemas.ts`, `trace-replay-schemas.ts`, and `api-document.json`.

Run `npm run validate --workspace=factorize-docs` to verify the generated artifact, parsed operation contract, and Mintlify configuration before publishing.

## REST operations
Contract: https://docs.factorize.sh/openapi.yaml
The site renders this exact generated contract under Reference → REST operations.

## Optional self-hosting
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/self-hosting/deployment

Hosted users can start at [app.factorize.sh](https://app.factorize.sh) without deploying anything. Self-hosting is for operators who want to own the application infrastructure.

The Worker lives in `packages/api`, React frontend in `packages/app`, and generated public client in `packages/api-client`. Use Node 24 and the root lockfile. Follow the [API-first deployment and rollback gates](https://github.com/GenerationSoftware/factorize/blob/main/docs/package-migration.md) before deploying static assets. Preserve Worker identity, bindings, migrations, and old hashed assets.

Install dependencies with `npm ci`. Configure `packages/api/wrangler.jsonc`, PostgreSQL, OAuth KV and artifact storage, set the final HTTPS `APP_ORIGIN`, then build with `npm run build:app` and deploy with `npm run deploy:app`. See [configuration](https://docs.factorize.sh/self-hosting/configuration) before deployment.

For local development, copy `packages/api/.dev.vars.example` to `packages/api/.dev.vars`, supply local configuration, and use `npm run dev`. Development uses HTTPS at `https://localhost:5173`; use that origin for local callbacks. The migration guide covers local database setup. Never commit secrets.

## Operator configuration
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/self-hosting/configuration

These steps apply only to your own deployment. Hosted Factorize users connect existing accounts in [Integrations](https://app.factorize.sh/integrations); they do not register Factorize OAuth applications or set Worker secrets.

Register provider applications for your deployment origin. Linear requires Issues and Issue labels webhooks and fresh workspace authorization after subscription changes; ClickUp registers its task webhook on connection. Configure the GitHub App credentials and webhook settings for your deployment using the template in `packages/api/.dev.vars.example` and the executable callbacks/webhook routes in `packages/api/src/worker.ts`.

## Account authentication

Factorize owns authentication in PostgreSQL. Create a native account at `/auth/signup` with an email address and a password of 12–200 characters. Emails are case-insensitive. Verify the email before signing in at `/auth/login`; email plus password are accepted. Linear is connected after sign-in from **Integrations**, only for Linear-backed triggers.

Postmark sends one-hour, single-use verification and password-reset links. `/auth/verify/request` resends verification; `/auth/password-reset` handles recovery. Links never appear in application responses or logs. Passwords use salted PBKDF2-SHA-256. **Change password** in the account menu requires the current password. Password reset, password change and sign-out invalidate existing sessions via membership session versions, including delegated API credentials.

Before deploying, configure `POSTMARK_SERVER_TOKEN` as a **production GitHub environment secret**. The deployment copies it to a Worker secret; the verified sender and transactional message stream are non-secret Worker vars in `packages/api/wrangler.jsonc`. For a manual Postmark preflight, set the following environment variables along with `APP_ORIGIN`:

| Setting | Required value |
| --- | --- |
| `POSTMARK_SERVER_TOKEN` | Postmark **server** API token for the sending server; never an account token or a committed value |
| `POSTMARK_FROM_EMAIL` | Plain email address on a verified Postmark sender signature or verified domain |
| `POSTMARK_MESSAGE_STREAM` | Active **transactional** stream ID, commonly `outbound` |

`APP_ORIGIN` must be the canonical HTTPS origin, without a trailing slash. Run `npm run auth:validate-email --workspace=factorize` manually when needed: it checks the server token/stream with Postmark and sends one preflight email from/to the configured sender, rejecting unverified senders or sending failures. It prints no credentials. Missing configuration fails the manual check. The deploy workflow does not run this check or send a preflight email. Runtime signup and recovery also fail closed if configuration or delivery fails; users can resend verification after a delivery failure. Local mail testing needs an HTTPS origin and a separate Postmark test server/sender; automated tests mock Postmark and never send mail.

### Optional Google sign-in

Create a **Web application** OAuth client in Google Cloud. Register exactly
`<APP_ORIGIN>/oauth/google/sign-in/callback` as an authorized redirect URI
(`https://app.factorize.sh/oauth/google/sign-in/callback` on the hosted deployment).
Complete Google's OAuth consent screen setup for your intended audience. Set
`GOOGLE_SIGN_IN_CLIENT_ID` and `GOOGLE_SIGN_IN_CLIENT_SECRET` as Worker secrets.
The Google button is hidden unless both values are set. Apply migration 0104
using the normal database deployment step. Google sign-in is separate from
Factorize's MCP authorization clients and uses only `openid email`.

A first Google sign-in matching an existing verified Factorize account
requires its current Factorize password; email alone never links accounts.
New Google users choose a unique Factorize username. For addresses Google
does not manage directly, Factorize emails a confirmation link to be opened
in the browser that started signup. Once signed in, Google-first users can
use **Set password**. First confirm the linked Google account again, then open the
Factorize email link in that same browser. An email link alone cannot establish a
first password on a Google account.

Addresses verified independently by Factorize are not replaced by Google.
For accounts enrolled using Google's authoritative email, Google remains the
authority for password recovery even after a password is added. Factorize
retires the old email's recovery authority and outstanding links when a Google
address change is observed. If the new address needs independent confirmation,
prove it through the Google recovery flow. If it is already used by another
Factorize account, password recovery pauses rather than transferring or combining
accounts. Sign-in with the linked Google account still works. Keep Postmark
configured for address confirmation and password recovery.

### Optional two-factor authentication

Two-factor authentication is off by default and configured by each user in
**Account settings → Two-factor authentication**. There is no team enforcement.
Set `TOTP_ENCRYPTION_KEY` as an independent Worker secret before offering
enrollment. Generate 32 cryptographically random bytes encoded as base64 (for
example, using `openssl rand -base64 32`). Do not reuse the credential encryption
key or store the value in the repository. Normal deployment applies migration
0105. Keep the key securely backed up; changing it without re-encrypting
existing TOTP secrets breaks authenticator verification for enrolled users.
Users with a saved recovery code can still sign in.

Enrollment requires confirmation of the current Factorize password, or fresh
Google confirmation for Google-only users. The setup QR code is generated in
the browser without sending the secret to a QR service. Users confirm a valid
authenticator code to enable 2FA and should immediately save the ten recovery
codes, which are shown once and work once each. Disabling requires primary
confirmation plus an authenticator or recovery code. Password reset does not
disable 2FA. Enable and disable invalidate older sessions and delegated grants
using existing membership session versions.

### Existing account migration

Apply `0008_native_accounts.sql` and `0009_remove_auth_usernames.sql` before deploying this code. They reject ambiguous legacy emails that differ only in case (reconcile those identities before retrying migration), preserve tenant IDs, memberships, triggers and encrypted Linear connections, and backfill explicit Linear organization-to-workspace mappings. Existing Linear-only users choose **Forgot password or previously signed in with Linear?**, receive a reset email at their existing address, and set a password. Email possession is required; signup cannot replace an existing account's credentials. Existing native users keep their passwords and may sign in by email; unverified accounts must verify first. A reset never promotes a member to owner. An account with multiple existing owner memberships currently opens the oldest workspace; no new workspace-switching UI is introduced.

Linear OAuth requires an authenticated owner, binds state to that user/workspace, stores the connection there, and never creates a Factorize session. A Linear organization already bound to another workspace cannot be claimed. Existing webhook routes resolve the explicit mapping. Do not delete that binding to work around an account-recovery problem.

### Authentication verification

`npm run check` runs unit/contract tests and Postmark preflight tests. CI also runs the real PostgreSQL authentication suite against a disposable service. To run it locally, set `AUTH_TEST_DATABASE_URL` to an isolated PostgreSQL server whose user can create/drop test databases, then run `npm test --workspace=factorize -- --run test/native-auth.postgres.test.ts`. The suite creates and removes its own database and applies every migration, including a legacy connection fixture before the auth migration.

## Configure Linear

Use authorization-code OAuth and enable **Webhooks** on the OAuth application. Configure:

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Callback URL | `https://your-domain.example/auth/linear/callback` |
| Webhook URL | `https://your-domain.example/webhooks/linear` |
| Webhook events | **Issues** and **Issue labels** |
| Webhook secret | Store as `LINEAR_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_SECRET` |

After changing the webhook settings, re-authorize existing workspaces so Linear creates a fresh workspace subscription.

## Configure ClickUp

Create a ClickUp OAuth application with the callback URL `https://your-domain.example/auth/clickup/callback`, then store its client ID and secret in `CLICKUP_CLIENT_ID` and `CLICKUP_CLIENT_SECRET`. Connecting ClickUp from Integrations registers the signed task webhook automatically. ClickUp events can filter a list by status, tag, assignee, or creator; all configured rules must match.


## Configuration reference

| Variable | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `LINEAR_CLIENT_ID` | Linear OAuth client ID |
| `LINEAR_CLIENT_SECRET` | Linear OAuth client secret |
| `LINEAR_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_SECRET` | Verifies Linear webhook signatures |
| `CLICKUP_CLIENT_ID` | ClickUp OAuth client ID |
| `CLICKUP_CLIENT_SECRET` | ClickUp OAuth client secret; ClickUp also uses a per-installation webhook secret stored encrypted by Factorize |
| `CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` | Base64-encoded 32-byte key for encrypted credentials |
| `SESSION_SIGNING_SECRET` | Independent secret for signed browser sessions |
| `APP_ORIGIN` | Public Worker origin, configured in `packages/api/wrangler.jsonc` |
| `OAUTH_KV` | KV binding containing OAuth clients, grants, refresh tokens, and revocation state |

Never commit `.dev.vars` or production secret values. The included `.dev.vars.example` is a safe template.

## Operations
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/self-hosting/operations

Use the [deployment guide](https://docs.factorize.sh/self-hosting/deployment) and the repository's
package-migration runbook for release and rollback procedures. Keep API
migrations, generated OpenAPI, API client output, and static frontend aligned.

The API Worker processes schedules and inbound provider webhooks. Monitor Worker
errors, database connectivity, and provider delivery outcomes. Event occurrences
are durable database records; MCP notifications prompt clients to read them and
are not the persistence layer.

Before a release, run the repository's documented local validation against an
isolated database. Never point validation at production or a shared database.
